etymology: From the Greek parthenos, “virgin” or “maiden,” the ten waiting maidens of the Lord’s parable of watchfulness.
biblical_def: The parable of the ten virgins is the Lord Jesus Christ’s great word of warning that His people must watch and be ready for His coming. Then shall the kingdom of heaven be likened unto ten virgins, which took their lamps, and went forth to meet the bridegroom (Mat 25:1); and five of them were wise, and five were foolish (Mat 25:2). The wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps, but the foolish took none; and while the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept. At midnight the cry was made, Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him (Mat 25:6). Then the foolish, whose lamps were going out, sought to borrow oil, but were sent to buy for themselves; and while they went, the bridegroom came, and they that were ready went in with him to the marriage, and the door was shut (Mat 25:10). The dictionary marks this parable as a solemn picture of the great division at the last day between those truly prepared and those who only seemed so. The oil is no outward show but the inward grace of the Spirit, not borrowed at the last hour. So the Lord seals the parable with the standing charge: Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh (Mat 25:13). The wise are the elect, kept ready by grace; the foolish are the hypocrites, shut out for ever from the marriage of the Lamb.
webster_summary: The Lord’s parable of five wise and five foolish maidens awaiting the bridegroom, teaching watchfulness for His coming.
webster_full: THE TEN VIRGINS, the Lord’s parable of watchfulness for the bridegroom’s coming.
Five were wise and took oil in their vessels with their lamps.
Five were foolish and took no oil, and their lamps went out.
The bridegroom came, and the ready went in to the marriage, and the door was shut.
Its charge is, Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour.
scriptures: Mat 25:1
Then shall the kingdom of heaven be likened unto ten virgins, which took their lamps, and went forth to meet the bridegroom.
Mat 25:6
And at midnight there was a cry made, Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him.
And while they went to buy, the bridegroom came; and they that were ready went in with him to the marriage: and the door was shut.
Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh.
corruption_summary: A parable of Scripture; it teaches that grace cannot be borrowed at the last hour, and the unready are shut out of the marriage of the Lamb.
corruption_paragraphs: The ten virgins have drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving in the church’s memory as the Lord’s great call to watchfulness. The dictionary records the parable that the reader may mark the difference between true readiness and the empty show that is shut out at the last.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the oil of grace cannot be borrowed at the last hour, and that profession without the inward work of the Spirit will not stand in the day of Christ’s coming. The wise and foolish looked alike until midnight; but only they that were ready went in to the marriage, and the door was shut. So the saint is bidden to watch, for he knows neither the day nor the hour; and the parable warns every soul to seek the grace that makes ready, lest it knock at a shut door and hear the dreadful word, I know you not.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “virgin,” the parable names the ten maidens whose lamps tried the readiness of the church.
roots_lines: The Ten Virgins — from the Greek parthenos, “virgin” or “maiden.”
They went forth with their lamps to meet the bridegroom.
Five were wise, with oil; five were foolish, without.
The ready went in to the marriage, and the door was shut.
Its charge is to watch, for the day and hour are unknown.
usage: Like the foolish virgins, those who trust an empty profession find the door shut at the last.
Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh.
The oil of grace cannot be borrowed; each soul must have its own before the bridegroom comes.

etymology: From the Greek talanton, a great weight or sum of money, the trust committed to the servants in the Lord’s parable of stewardship.
biblical_def: The parable of the talents teaches that the Lord Jesus Christ, going away into a far country, commits to His servants a trust to be used for His glory until He returns, and will reckon with each according to his faithfulness. He delivered unto them his goods; unto one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to every man according to his several ability (Mat 25:15). The first two traded with their talents and gained as much again; but he that had received one went and digged in the earth, and hid his lord’s money (Mat 25:18). After a long time the lord returned and reckoned with them. To the faithful He said, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord (Mat 25:21). But the slothful servant, who had hidden his talent and charged his lord with hardness, was condemned as wicked and unprofitable, and cast into outer darkness. The dictionary marks this parable as the rule of Christian stewardship: every gift, office, and opportunity is a trust from the Lord, to be improved for Him. The faithful servant is not saved by his works but shows by them the grace that wrought in him; the slothful servant, hiding his trust, betrays a heart that never knew its Master. So the faithful enter into the joy of their Lord.
webster_summary: The Lord’s parable of servants entrusted with talents, teaching faithful stewardship and the reckoning at His return.
webster_full: THE TALENTS, the Lord’s parable of servants entrusted with His goods.
To each he gave according to his several ability, five, two, and one.
Two traded and gained; one hid his talent in the earth.
The faithful heard, Well done, thou good and faithful servant.
The slothful was cast as unprofitable into outer darkness.
scriptures: And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability; and straightway took his journey.
But he that had received one went and digged in the earth, and hid his lord’s money.
His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
For unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance: but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath.
corruption_summary: A parable of Scripture; it teaches that every gift is a trust from the Lord, to be improved for Him against the day of reckoning.
corruption_paragraphs: The talents have drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the Lord’s great parable of stewardship. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the reckoning that awaits every servant for the trust committed to him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that every gift, office, and opportunity is a trust from the Lord, to be improved for His glory until He comes. The faithful servants traded and gained, and entered into the joy of their lord; the slothful hid his trust and was cast out, his unfaithfulness betraying a heart that never truly knew its Master. So the parable teaches that good works do not earn salvation but flow from the grace that wrought within, and that the day of reckoning will divide the faithful from the false. Let every soul use what God has given, that it may hear, Well done, thou good and faithful servant.
roots_summary: From the Greek for a weight of money, the parable names the trust committed to the servants of Christ.
roots_lines: The Talents — from the Greek talanton, a great weight or sum of money.
The lord delivered his goods to his servants before his journey.
Each received according to his several ability.
Two traded and gained; one hid his talent.
The faithful entered the joy of their lord; the slothful was cast out.
usage: Like the faithful servants, the saint trades with the trust his Lord has given.
Well done, thou good and faithful servant: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
Every gift is a stewardship, and the slothful who hides his trust is cast out.

etymology: From the Greek mna, a pound or unit of money, the trust given to the servants in the Lord’s parable of occupying until He come.
biblical_def: The parable of the pounds was spoken by the Lord Jesus Christ as He drew near to Jerusalem, because the people thought that the kingdom of God should immediately appear (Luk 19:11). A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom, and to return; and he called his ten servants, and delivered them ten pounds, and said unto them, Occupy till I come (Luk 19:13). His citizens hated him and sent a message after him, We will not have this man to reign over us; yet he received the kingdom and returned to reckon with his servants. He that gained ten pounds was set over ten cities, and he that gained five over five; but the servant who hid his pound in a napkin and charged his lord with austerity was condemned out of his own mouth, and his pound given to him that had ten. The dictionary marks this parable as the Lord’s charge to His servants in the long interval before His kingdom is openly revealed: they are to occupy, that is, to trade and labour faithfully, till He come. The rebel citizens, who would not have Him reign, picture the Jews and all who reject His lordship, and their doom is told: those mine enemies, bring hither, and slay them before me (Luk 19:27). So the parable joins the call to faithful service with the certainty of Christ’s return to reward His own and to judge His foes.
webster_summary: The Lord’s parable of the nobleman who bade his servants occupy till he come, rewarding the faithful and judging his foes.
webster_full: THE POUNDS, the Lord’s parable of the nobleman who went to receive a kingdom.
He gave his ten servants ten pounds and said, Occupy till I come.
His citizens said, We will not have this man to reign over us.
The faithful who traded were set over cities; the slothful lost his pound.
The rebel citizens were slain before him at his return.
scriptures: And as they heard these things, he added and spake a parable, because he was nigh to Jerusalem, and because they thought that the kingdom of God should immediately appear.
And he called his ten servants, and delivered them ten pounds, and said unto them, Occupy till I come.
And he said unto him, Well, thou good servant: because thou hast been faithful in a very little, have thou authority over ten cities.
But those mine enemies, which would not that I should reign over them, bring hither, and slay them before me.
corruption_summary: A parable of Scripture; it charges the servants of Christ to occupy faithfully till He come, and warns that His enemies shall be judged.
corruption_paragraphs: The pounds have drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the Lord’s charge to labour faithfully until His return. The dictionary records the parable that the reader may mark both the reward of the faithful and the doom of those who would not have Him reign.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the charge to occupy till He come: the Lord, gone to receive His kingdom, has left His servants to trade faithfully with what He has entrusted to them in the long interval before His open reign. The faithful are set over cities, rewarded above their labour; the slothful loses even what he had; and the citizens who would not have Him reign are slain before Him. So the parable joins diligent service with the certainty of Christ’s return, and warns that to reject His lordship is to perish under the King men despised but God enthroned.
roots_summary: From the Greek for a pound of money, the parable names the trust given to the servants who were to occupy till the Lord come.
roots_lines: The Pounds — from the Greek mna, a pound or unit of money.
A nobleman went to receive a kingdom and to return.
He gave his servants pounds and said, Occupy till I come.
The faithful were set over cities; the slothful lost his pound.
His enemies who refused his reign were slain before him.
usage: Like the servants of the parable, the saint is to occupy faithfully till the Lord come.
And he said unto them, Occupy till I come.
Those who will not have Christ reign over them shall be judged at His return.

etymology: From the Greek deipnon, “supper” or “feast,” the great banquet of the Lord’s parable of the gospel call.
biblical_def: The parable of the great supper sets forth the free and gracious call of the gospel, and the guilt of those who slight it. A certain man made a great supper, and bade many; and sent his servant at supper time to say to them that were bidden, Come; for all things are now ready (Luk 14:17). But they all with one consent began to make excuse: one had bought a piece of ground, another five yoke of oxen, another had married a wife, and could not come. The master of the house, being angry, sent his servant out into the streets and lanes of the city to bring in the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind; and yet there was room, so he commanded, Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled (Luk 14:23). The dictionary marks this parable as a picture of God’s gracious invitation in the gospel, first to the Jews who had been bidden, and then, when they refused, to the poor and the outcast and the Gentiles in the highways. The excuses are not great crimes but lawful things loved more than Christ, and they damn as surely; for the Lord declares, None of those men which were bidden shall taste of my supper (Luk 14:24). The compelling is no force upon the will, but the effectual drawing of grace, by which the unwilling are made willing and brought in.
webster_summary: The Lord’s parable of the great feast whose bidden guests made excuse, and the poor were compelled to come in.
webster_full: THE GREAT SUPPER, the Lord’s parable of the gospel call to a great feast.
The bidden guests all made excuse and would not come.
The master sent for the poor, the maimed, the halt, and the blind.
He bade his servant compel them to come in, that his house might be filled.
None of the bidden who refused should taste of his supper.
scriptures: And sent his servant at supper time to say to them that were bidden, Come; for all things are now ready.
And they all with one consent began to make excuse. The first said unto him, I have bought a piece of ground, and I must needs go and see it: I pray thee have me excused.
And the lord said unto the servant, Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled.
For I say unto you, That none of those men which were bidden shall taste of my supper.
corruption_summary: A parable of Scripture; it sets forth the free gospel call, the guilt of slighting it, and the effectual grace that compels the outcast to come in.
corruption_paragraphs: The great supper has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the Lord’s great picture of the gospel feast and the call to come. The dictionary records the parable that the reader may mark both the guilt of the excusers and the grace that fills the house.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the gospel call is free and full, all things now ready, yet slighted by men who love lawful things more than Christ. The bidden made excuse and were shut out; the poor and the outcast were gathered in; and the servant was charged to compel them to come in. This compelling is no violence upon the will but the powerful, effectual drawing of sovereign grace, by which the unwilling are made willing and brought to the feast. So the parable warns that to make excuse is to perish, and teaches that all who come, come because they are drawn.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “supper,” the parable names the great feast of the gospel from which the excusers were shut out.
roots_lines: The Great Supper — from the Greek deipnon, “supper” or “feast.”
A man made a great supper and bade many.
The bidden guests all made excuse and would not come.
The poor and outcast were gathered in their stead.
The servant was bidden to compel them to come in.
usage: Like the bidden of the great supper, those who make excuse shall not taste the feast.
Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in.
The compelling of grace makes the unwilling willing and brings them in to the feast.

etymology: From the Greek gamos, “marriage” or “wedding,” the king’s wedding feast for his son in the Lord’s parable of the kingdom.
biblical_def: The parable of the marriage feast sets forth the kingdom of heaven under the figure of a king which made a marriage for his son (Mat 22:2), and the dreadful guilt of those who spurn his invitation. The king sent his servants to call them that were bidden, but they would not come; and when he sent other servants, saying, all things are ready: come unto the marriage (Mat 22:4), they made light of it, and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise; and the rest took his servants, and entreated them spitefully, and slew them. The king was wroth, and sent forth his armies, and destroyed those murderers, and burned up their city. Then he sent his servants into the highways to gather all that they found, both bad and good, and the wedding was furnished with guests. The dictionary marks this parable as the history of the gospel call to the Jewish nation, which not only refused but slew the prophets and the apostles, and was visited with the burning of Jerusalem; and of the call going forth to the Gentiles in the highways, that the feast might be filled. So the Scripture teaches that to despise the King’s gracious invitation to His Son’s marriage is no small thing, but a contempt that kindles wrath; and that when the bidden prove unworthy, God in sovereign grace gathers a people from the streets and lanes to honour His Son.
webster_summary: The Lord’s parable of the king’s marriage feast for his son, refused by the bidden and filled from the highways.
webster_full: THE MARRIAGE FEAST, the Lord’s parable of a king’s wedding for his son.
The bidden guests would not come, and made light of the call.
Some slew the servants, and the king destroyed them and burned their city.
He sent into the highways to gather guests, both bad and good.
The wedding was furnished with guests from the streets and lanes.
scriptures: Mat 22:2
The kingdom of heaven is like unto a certain king, which made a marriage for his son,
Mat 22:4
Again, he sent forth other servants, saying, Tell them which are bidden, Behold, I have prepared my dinner: my oxen and my fatlings are killed, and all things are ready: come unto the marriage.
Mat 22:8
Then saith he to his servants, The wedding is ready, but they which were bidden were not worthy.
Mat 22:9
Go ye therefore into the highways, and as many as ye shall find, bid to the marriage.
corruption_summary: A parable of Scripture; it traces the gospel call to the Jews who refused, the judgment on their city, and the gathering of a people from the highways.
corruption_paragraphs: The marriage feast has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the Lord’s parable of the king’s invitation refused. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the guilt of those who despise the gracious call and the grace that fills the feast in their stead.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that to spurn the King’s gracious call to His Son’s marriage kindles wrath. The bidden made light of the feast, and some slew the servants, and the king destroyed them and burned their city, as Jerusalem was burned for rejecting the gospel and slaying the prophets and apostles. Then the call went into the highways, and the wedding was furnished with guests gathered from the streets, both bad and good, picturing the Gentiles brought in by sovereign grace. So the parable teaches that God will have His Son honoured at His marriage, and that the despisers perish while the unworthy are gathered in.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “marriage,” the parable names the king’s wedding feast for his son in the kingdom of heaven.
roots_lines: The Marriage Feast — from the Greek gamos, “marriage” or “wedding.”
A king made a marriage for his son and bade many.
The bidden refused, and some slew his servants.
The king destroyed them and burned their city.
He gathered guests from the highways to fill the feast.
usage: Like the bidden of the marriage feast, those who despise the King’s call bring wrath upon themselves.
The wedding is ready, but they which were bidden were not worthy.
When the bidden refuse, God gathers a people from the highways to honour His Son.

etymology: From the Greek endyma, “garment” or “raiment,” the wedding robe whose lack cast out the unfit guest in the Lord’s parable.
biblical_def: The parable of the wedding garment, joined to the marriage feast, sets forth that no man may stand in the kingdom of God clothed in his own righteousness, but only in the righteousness God provides. When the king came in to see the guests gathered from the highways, he saw there a man which had not on a wedding garment; and he saith unto him, Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless (Mat 22:11; Mat 22:12). Then the king commanded his servants, Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Mat 22:13). The dictionary marks this garment as a figure of the imputed righteousness of Christ, the fine linen, clean and white, which is the righteousness of saints (Rev 19:8), without which no sinner is meet to sit at the marriage of the Lamb. The man came in among the called, professing as the rest, but had not put on Christ; and when the King searched, his own clothing condemned him, and he was speechless, having no plea. So the Scripture teaches that a place among the visible church and the outward call avails nothing without the wedding robe of imputed righteousness, and the parable closes with the great word, For many are called, but few are chosen (Mat 22:14).
webster_summary: The Lord’s parable of the guest cast out for want of a wedding garment, teaching the necessity of imputed righteousness.
webster_full: THE WEDDING GARMENT, the robe whose lack cast a guest from the marriage feast.
The king found a man who had not on a wedding garment.
Asked how he came in without it, the man was speechless.
He was bound and cast into outer darkness.
Its lesson is, Many are called, but few are chosen.
scriptures: And when the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man which had not on a wedding garment:
And he saith unto him, Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless.
Then said the king to the servants, Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
For many are called, but few are chosen.
corruption_summary: A parable of Scripture; it teaches that none may stand at the marriage of the Lamb save in the imputed righteousness of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The wedding garment has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the Lord’s figure of the righteousness without which none may sit at His feast. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the necessity of the robe Christ provides.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that no sinner may stand in the kingdom clothed in his own righteousness, but only in the wedding garment God provides, which is the imputed righteousness of Christ, the fine linen, clean and white, the righteousness of saints. The man came in among the called, professing as the rest, but had not put on Christ; and when the King searched, he was speechless, having no plea. So the parable warns that a place in the visible church and the outward call avail nothing without the robe of imputed righteousness; for many are called, but few are chosen.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “garment,” the parable names the wedding robe of imputed righteousness without which none may sit at the feast.
roots_lines: The Wedding Garment — from the Greek endyma, “garment” or “raiment.”
The king found a guest without the wedding garment.
Questioned, the man was speechless and had no plea.
He was bound and cast into outer darkness.
Its lesson is that many are called, but few are chosen.
usage: Like the man without the wedding garment, the merely professing are cast out at the last.
Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless.
None may sit at the marriage of the Lamb save clothed in the imputed righteousness of Christ.

etymology: From the Greek ergates, “labourer” or “workman,” the hired workers of the Lord’s parable of sovereign grace in the vineyard.
biblical_def: The parable of the labourers in the vineyard sets forth the sovereign freedom of God’s grace, which gives not by debt but of His own good pleasure. A householder went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard, and agreed with them for a penny a day; and he went out again about the third, the sixth, the ninth, and the eleventh hours, and hired more, saying, Whatsoever is right I will give you. When even was come, the lord of the vineyard bade his steward give every man a penny, beginning from the last unto the first. They which were hired first murmured, supposing they should have received more; but the householder answered, Friend, I do thee no wrong: didst not thou agree with me for a penny? (Mat 20:13). Take that thine is, and go thy way: I will give unto this last, even as unto thee. The dictionary marks this parable as a rebuke to all murmuring against the freeness of grace. God gives no man less than is just, but to whom He will He gives more, of His mere bounty; and none may charge Him with wrong. The closing words pierce the envious heart: Is thine eye evil, because I am good? (Mat 20:15). So the Scripture teaches that salvation is of grace, not of merit; and that the last shall be first, and the first last, for many be called, but few chosen.
webster_summary: The Lord’s parable of the householder who paid all his labourers alike, teaching the sovereign freedom of grace.
webster_full: THE LABORERS IN THE VINEYARD, the Lord’s parable of sovereign grace.
A householder hired labourers at the first hour and through the day.
At even he gave every man a penny, the last as the first.
The first murmured, but he said, Is thine eye evil, because I am good?
Its lesson is that the last shall be first, and the first last.
scriptures: Mat 20:1
For the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard.
But he answered one of them, and said, Friend, I do thee no wrong: didst not thou agree with me for a penny?
Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good?
So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen.
corruption_summary: A parable of Scripture; it teaches the sovereign freedom of God’s grace, which none may charge with wrong.
corruption_paragraphs: The labourers in the vineyard have drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the Lord’s great parable of free and sovereign grace. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the rebuke it gives to every murmur against the goodness of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God gives not by debt but of His own good pleasure. He wrongs no man, paying each the wage agreed; but to whom He will He gives more, of His mere bounty, and none may charge Him with injustice. The first labourers murmured at His liberality to the last, and He answered, Is thine eye evil, because I am good? So the parable rebukes the envious heart that would bind grace to merit or seniority, and teaches that salvation is wholly of grace; for the last shall be first, and the first last, and the LORD doeth what He will with His own.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “labourer,” the parable names the workers paid alike to teach the sovereign freedom of grace.
roots_lines: The Laborers in the Vineyard — from the Greek ergates, “labourer” or “workman.”
A householder hired labourers through the hours of the day.
At even he paid every man a penny alike.
The first murmured at his liberality to the last.
He answered, Is thine eye evil, because I am good?
usage: Like the first labourers, the murmuring heart begrudges God the freeness of His grace.
Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good?
Salvation is of grace, not of merit; the last shall be first, and the first last.

etymology: From the Greek teknon, “child” or “son,” the two sons of the Lord’s parable of obedience in deed and word.
biblical_def: The parable of the two sons, spoken to the chief priests and elders in the temple, sets forth that true obedience is in the deed and not the word only. A certain man had two sons; he came to the first, and said, Son, go work to day in my vineyard. He answered and said, I will not: but afterward he repented, and went (Mat 21:29). And he came to the second, and said likewise; and he answered and said, I go, sir: and went not (Mat 21:30). Then the Lord asked, Whether of them twain did the will of his father? and they said, The first; and He turned the word against them. The dictionary marks this parable as a sharp rebuke to the religious leaders of Israel, who said with their mouths, I go, sir, professing obedience to God, yet went not, but rejected His counsel; while the publicans and harlots, who had once said, I will not, repented at the preaching of John and entered the kingdom. So the Lord declared, the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you (Mat 21:31). The Scripture teaches by this that mere profession, the fair word without the obedient deed, is hypocrisy; and that the publicans, repenting and obeying, are accepted before the chief priests, who professed and obeyed not. Not the sayers but the doers of God’s will shall enter; for repentance that bears fruit in obedience is the mark of the true child.
webster_summary: The Lord’s parable of two sons bidden to the vineyard, teaching obedience in deed above word.
webster_full: THE TWO SONS, the Lord’s parable of obedience in deed and word.
The first said, I will not, but afterward repented and went.
The second said, I go, sir, and went not.
The first did the will of his father.
The publicans and harlots go into the kingdom before the professing leaders.
scriptures: But what think ye? A certain man had two sons; and he came to the first, and said, Son, go work to day in my vineyard.
He answered and said, I will not: but afterward he repented, and went.
And he came to the second, and said likewise. And he answered and said, I go, sir: and went not.
Whether of them twain did the will of his father? They say unto him, The first. Jesus saith unto them, Verily I say unto you, That the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you.
corruption_summary: A parable of Scripture; it teaches that true obedience is in the deed, and that repentance bearing fruit accepts the publican before the professing hypocrite.
corruption_paragraphs: The two sons have drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the Lord’s sharp parable of obedience in deed above word. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the difference between the fair word and the obedient life.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that obedience is in the deed and not the word only. The first son refused, then repented and went; the second professed, I go, sir, and went not; and the first did the will of his father. So the Lord rebuked the chief priests, who professed obedience yet rejected His counsel, while the publicans and harlots repented at John’s preaching and entered the kingdom before them. The parable warns that mere profession without obedience is hypocrisy, and teaches that repentance bearing the fruit of obedience is the mark of the true child of God.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “son,” the parable names the two sons whose answers tried the difference between word and deed.
roots_lines: The Two Sons — from the Greek teknon, “child” or “son.”
A man bade his two sons work in his vineyard.
The first refused, then repented and went.
The second professed, and went not.
The first did the will of his father.
usage: Like the second son, the mere professor says, I go, sir, and goes not.
He answered and said, I will not: but afterward he repented, and went.
Not the sayers but the doers of the will of God shall enter the kingdom.

etymology: From the Greek georgos, “husbandman” or “vine-dresser,” the wicked tenants of the Lord’s parable of the rejected Son.
biblical_def: The parable of the wicked husbandmen sets forth Israel’s long rejection of the prophets and at last of the Son Himself, and the taking of the kingdom from the unfaithful nation. A householder planted a vineyard, set a hedge about it, and let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country (Mat 21:33). When the fruit drew near, he sent his servants to receive the fruits, but the husbandmen beat one, killed another, and stoned a third; and so with more servants. Last of all he sent unto them his son, saying, They will reverence my son. But the husbandmen said, This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance; and they caught him, and cast him out of the vineyard, and slew him (Mat 21:38; Mat 21:39). The Lord asked what the lord of the vineyard would do, and answered His own question: He will miserably destroy those wicked men, and let out his vineyard unto other husbandmen. The dictionary marks the husbandmen as the rulers of Israel, who slew the prophets and crucified the Son; and the sentence is plain: Therefore say I unto you, The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof (Mat 21:43). So the Scripture sets forth Christ as the rejected Son, who is become the head stone of the corner, the LORD’s doing, marvellous in our eyes (Psa 118:22).
webster_summary: The Lord’s parable of the tenants who slew the servants and the heir, whose vineyard was taken and given to others.
webster_full: THE WICKED HUSBANDMEN, the Lord’s parable of the rejected Son.
A householder let out his vineyard and sent for the fruits.
The husbandmen beat, killed, and stoned his servants.
Last he sent his son, and they slew the heir.
The vineyard was taken and given to a nation bringing forth fruit.
scriptures: Hear another parable: There was a certain householder, which planted a vineyard, and hedged it round about, and digged a winepress in it, and built a tower, and let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country:
But when the husbandmen saw the son, they said among themselves, This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance.

Jesus saith unto them, Did ye never read in the scriptures, The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner: this is the Lord’s doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes?
Therefore say I unto you, The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof.
corruption_summary: A parable of Scripture; it sets forth the rejected Son, the judgment on the nation, and the kingdom given to a people bringing forth fruit.
corruption_paragraphs: The wicked husbandmen have drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the Lord’s parable of the rejected Son and the kingdom taken from the unfaithful. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the guilt of those who slew the heir and the grace that gives the vineyard to a fruitful people.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Christ is the rejected Son who is become the head stone of the corner. The husbandmen, who are the rulers of Israel, slew the prophets and at last the Son Himself, saying, This is the heir; come, let us kill him; and for this the kingdom was taken from the nation and given to a people bringing forth the fruits thereof. So the parable sets forth both the judgment on those who reject the Son and the LORD’s marvellous doing in exalting the stone the builders refused, that He might be the corner of the house of God.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “husbandman,” the parable names the wicked tenants who slew the heir and lost the vineyard.
roots_lines: The Wicked Husbandmen — from the Greek georgos, “husbandman” or “vine-dresser.”
A householder let out his vineyard to husbandmen.
They beat and slew the servants he sent for the fruits.
Last they slew his son, the heir.
The vineyard was given to a nation bringing forth fruit.
usage: Like the wicked husbandmen, those who reject the Son lose the inheritance they coveted.
This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance.
The stone which the builders rejected is become the head of the corner.

etymology: From the Greek oikodespotes, “master of a house,” the instructed scribe of the Lord’s parable who brings forth treasure new and old.
biblical_def: The parable of the householder, the briefest of the Lord’s kingdom parables, sets forth the instructed disciple as a steward of divine truth. When the Lord had spoken the parables of the kingdom and asked, Have ye understood all these things? they said unto Him, Yea, Lord. Then said He unto them, Therefore every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old (Mat 13:52). The dictionary marks this householder as the picture of every faithful teacher in the church, the scribe taught of God, whose mind is a treasury furnished from the Scriptures. He brings forth things old, the law and the prophets, the ancient revelation of the LORD; and things new, the gospel of the kingdom now opened in Christ; and he shows the two to be one treasure, for the new is the fulfilling of the old, and the old is the promise of the new. So the Scripture teaches that the minister of the word is no mere reservoir but a dispenser, bringing forth from his store as the household has need. He is instructed unto the kingdom, taught by the Spirit to understand and to teach; and his treasure is not his own invention but the deposit of truth committed to him, old and new together, that he may feed the people of God with the whole counsel of the LORD.
webster_summary: The Lord’s parable of the instructed scribe, likened to a householder bringing treasure new and old.
webster_full: THE HOUSEHOLDER, the Lord’s parable of the instructed scribe of the kingdom.
Every scribe instructed unto the kingdom is like a householder.
He bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old.
The old is the law and prophets; the new is the gospel of the kingdom.
He is a steward dispensing the whole counsel of God.
scriptures: Then said he unto them, Therefore every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old.
Jesus saith unto them, Have ye understood all these things? They say unto him, Yea, Lord.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
He answered and said unto them, Because it is given unto you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it is not given.
corruption_summary: A parable of Scripture; it sets forth the instructed teacher as a steward bringing forth from his treasure things new and old.
corruption_paragraphs: The householder has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the Lord’s figure of the instructed scribe of the kingdom. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the office of the faithful teacher, whose treasure is the whole counsel of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the minister of the word is a steward bringing forth out of his treasure things new and old. The scribe instructed unto the kingdom holds the old, the law and the prophets, and the new, the gospel now opened in Christ, and shows them to be one treasure, the new fulfilling the old and the old promising the new. He is no mere reservoir but a dispenser, feeding the household as it has need. So the parable teaches that sound teaching is not invention but the faithful bringing forth of the deposit of truth committed to the church, rightly divided for the people of God.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “master of a house,” the parable names the instructed scribe who brings forth treasure new and old.
roots_lines: The Householder — from the Greek oikodespotes, “master of a house.”
Every scribe instructed unto the kingdom is like a householder.
He brings forth out of his treasure things new and old.
The old is the law and prophets; the new is the gospel.
He is a steward dispensing the whole counsel of God.
usage: Like the householder, the instructed teacher brings forth treasure both new and old.
Every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a householder.
The faithful minister dispenses the deposit of truth, the old fulfilled in the new.
